[11/23/26, 7:27:52 AM] Meta AI: Yes — that correction matters, and I got it slightly wrong in my last message. It's not "increment the rightmost digit."

77777511111  // first time 5 appears

...
`5 → 6` is an increment at _that_ position. All the faster digits to the right go back to `11111`, their start. That's the whole odometer rule:
incrementAtPosition(p):
  positions[p] += 1
  for q > p: positions[q] = 1   // reset, don't keep counting
What the code did was naively increment at the _next_ contradiction — `...11112` — as if the `5` was still fixed. It never did the `5 → 6` step, and it never reset the right part. And that same rule covers both cases:

- *Failure at `p`:* `incrementAtPosition(p)` — try the next value at `p`, reset right.
- *Success at `p`:* yield it, then `incrementAtPosition(p)` — try the next success at `p`, reset right.
- *Contradiction with a left, slower node at `p_left`:* `incrementAtPosition(p_left)` — changing the right can't help, so you jump straight to the left increment and reset the whole right block. That's your cutoff.

So the odometer is one function, used in three places. The code only had the first one, and only partially.

On the refactor — your accumulator idea is the right fit for generators:

- `pos/neg` accumulator propagates *down* as you go into a subproblem, so the child sees the prefix.
- Successful results propagate *horizontally* — the child yields a complete `pos/neg`, the parent tries it, and if it fails downstream, the parent asks the child for the _next_ yield, not for a fresh solve.

Two traps from Enigma-style generator debugging, exactly the one you named:

1. *Yield a copy, not the live accumulator.* If you `yield pos` and then mutate `pos` for the next candidate, the parent holding the previous yield sees it change under it. `yield [...pos]` / `yield [...neg]`, or make the accumulator persistent/immutable.
2. *`while(true)` by not yielding.* If a branch can loop without a `yield` — e.g. it increments the odometer but never yields a success or a failure to the parent — the generator spins forever and looks like a hang. Every `incrementAtPosition` path has to either yield or terminate. That's the easiest bug to introduce when you convert `return` to `yield`.

If you do that — odometer with `incrementAtPosition(p) + reset right`, generator yielding copied `pos/neg`, accumulator down / successes sideways — then the theory you already have becomes the code.

[11/23/26, 7:28:41 AM] Meta AI: You're right — I mis-stated it. Thank you for catching it.

*Not "increment at the position that just resolved." Increment at the position that just _failed_.*

Success doesn't increment anything. Success yields and _suspends_:
solve(p) -> yield success

// parent tries the rest under that success
The next increment only happens when something downstream *fails*, and it happens at the _failing_ position:
rest fails, failure attributed to p_left
→ incrementAtPosition(p_left)
→ reset everything to the right of p_left to 11111
So your sequence is:

// rest fails, failure is attributed to 5
77777611111  // 5 → 6, right resets
77777611112
77777611113
`5 → 6` happens because `5` *failed* — in the context of the rest — not because it resolved. If the rest had succeeded, you'd never have incremented `5` at all. You'd be done.

That's why the old code was wrong in the other direction: it incremented at the _next contradiction_ — the downstream failure — as if that downstream position was the one to change, without attributing the failure back to the left position that actually caused it, and without resetting the right.

Corrected rule, one function:
onFailure(p_fail):
  positions[p_fail] += 1
  for q > p_fail: positions[q] = 1
No increment on success. Success just yields. Failure drives the odometer.

That keeps your left-cutoff too: if the failure is attributed to a left, slower node, you increment _there_ and wipe the whole right block — because changing the right can't fix a left failure.

[11/23/26, 7:35:34 AM] Meta AI: Yes — that's the reconciliation, and your snippet is exactly right. I was collapsing two different increments into one.

There are *two* uses of `incrementAtPosition`, same function, different argument:

*1. Success — default counting, `incrementAtPosition(0)`*

After you yield a success, when the generator is resumed, you just count normally:
while (true) {
  attempts++
  const result = solveRest()

  if (result.map) {
    yield finish(and(...[...extra, ...result]))  // <-- not return
    incrementAtPosition(0)  // odometer + 1, continue counting
    continue
  }
  if (!incrementAtPosition(result)) break;  // failure path
}
That's the `77777611111 → 77777611112 → 77777611113` counting. Success doesn't jump. It yields, then on resume does the normal `+1` at position `0`. The `0` is the rightmost, fastest digit — so this is "give me the next success in order."

*2. Failure — jump, `incrementAtPosition(result)`*

`result` here is the failing position. If the failure is attributed to a left, slower node, you increment _there_ and reset everything to its right to `11111`. That's the `77777511111 → 77777611111` jump. You don't keep counting `...11112` under a `5` that already failed.

So:

- Success: `yield`, then `incrementAtPosition(0)` on resume.
- Failure: `incrementAtPosition(failingPosition)`, no yield.

And your second change is what makes (1) work:
// before: single success, commits
const res = solve(x, tryOuterAndPositive, tryOuterAndNegative, positions[i], nesting + 1)

// after: stream of successes, backtracks on demand
for (const res of solve(x, tryOuterAndPositive, tryOuterAndNegative, positions[i], nesting + 1)) {
  // try res against the rest
  // if rest fails, loop asks for the next res
  // which resumes the child generator, which does its incrementAtPosition(0)
}
The `for...of` _is_ the "continue after finding successful sequence." The parent doesn't have to manually increment the child — resuming the generator does it, via that `incrementAtPosition(0)` after the `yield`.

That's why it's a small change in shape but a real refactor in effect: every `const res = solve(...)` becomes `for (res of solve(...))`, and every `return finish(...)` in a success path becomes `yield finish(...)` + `incrementAtPosition(0)`.

And the one trap in your snippet: `yield finish(...)` has to yield a _copy_ of `pos/neg`. If `finish` returns the live accumulator, the next `incrementAtPosition(0)` + next `solveRest()` will mutate the success you just yielded, and the parent will see it change under it.
